records.text: e BoJ will stay comfortably carry-positive in the current fiscal year but will likely fall into a small (about JPY0.3trn) negative carry position in the next fiscal year (see Figure 1). The implications of negative carry are subject to debate, even if theoretically a central bank does not have a cash-flow issue – usually phrased as: “just print more money”. However, from a fiscal point of view, losing ‘non-tax revenue’ from the BoJ, which was about JPY2trn per year from 2022 to 2025, is painful for the government, in our view (for our basic calculations, see Figure 3 overleaf). Primary income: Two sources make up most of the BoJ’s primary income: income from JGBs based on book value accounting; and dividends from ETF holdings. As the BoJ buys JPY24– 30trn/year of JGBs on a gross basis, the average yield is expected to rise, albeit modestly. Our analysis assumes a modest increase in the ETF dividend. In addition to primary income, the BoJ earns interest (basically the same rate as IOER) from its loan operation. While the balance of its Loan Support Program is due to fall to zero in 2028, the balance on its Loans for Climate Transition is likely to remain steady (currently JPY25trn), as banks actively apply to secure term funding in relation to the NSFR (Net Stable Funding Ratio). The family feud continued in earnest with three dissents to this meeting, as Logan, Hammack and Kashkari openly called for rate hikes (Figure 1). These are the same 3 voters who dissented in April on the grounds that the policy statement should encapsulate 2-way risk to the next policy move. Notably, all three dissenters represent a large and growing cohort of hawks (Figure 2). This of course means that the entire Board along with Williams and Paulson voted to maintain policy. As was the fashion at the June meeting, the statement itself was very short, characterizing the economy as solid, jobs as stable and inflation remaining elevated. While the presser was normal in length, we once again got very little policy insight from the Chair, as he avoided providing granularity on the Fed’s reaction function. The index is most positive when positioning is long on the pairs with the most positive carry and short on the pairs with the most negative carry, indicating crowded long carry positions. Conversely, long carry positions have scope to build when the index is close to 0 or negative. Figure 1 shows the index since 2016 while Figure 2 focuses on 2026. As USD longs have since retraced so has the carry-positioning index, which is now hovering around +4. What is the relationship between carry-positioning and carry returns? Our analysis shows that the carry-positioning index is useful for determining whether the carry trade still has scope to perform. Figure 3 shows the Sharpe ratios of the forward returns of a simple carry strategy that buys the top three currency pairs with the most positive carry and sells the top three currency pairs with the most negative carry, for different ranges of the carry-positioning index.
